title: Bhishma's vow
carry: a vow with witnesses is hard to take back

segments.voice: Yesterday: a father's half answer, and a son who quietly found the other half. A true reason, not the whole one.
screen: `A TRUE REASON, NOT THE WHOLE ONE.`

segments.voice: The heir to the throne comes to a fisherman's door, and he doesn't come alone. Devavrata brings old chiefs of the warrior class with him, elders whose word carries weight. He has come on his father's errand: to ask for the fisherman's daughter as a bride for King Shantanu. The fisherman receives them with honor. And then, politely, carefully, with all those elders listening, he tells the prince exactly what's wrong with the match.
screen: `A PRINCE AT A FISHERMAN'S DOOR.` → `ELDERS AS WITNESSES.` → `WHAT'S WRONG WITH THE MATCH.`

segments.voice: The fisherman starts with praise. This match, he says, is one anyone would want; to turn it down would be foolish. He has no quarrel with the king. But there is one fault, and he names it: a rival. Whoever has you as a rival, he tells Devavrata, god or demon, can never live happily for long. That's a bold thing for a fisherman to say to a warrior prince, the king's own heir, in front of witnesses. In effect: the problem is you. Your strength. Your claim. Any grandson of his would grow up in that shadow. And Devavrata doesn't argue. He doesn't say he'd never harm a child, or ask to be trusted. He answers the problem by removing it. Hear my vow, he says, before all these chiefs. The son born of her will be our king. I give up the throne. The place he gives up is heir apparent, yuvaraja, the one his father gave him when he brought him home from the river. Now, for his father's happiness, he hands it to a brother who isn't even born. Notice where he speaks it. Not in private, not to his father, but in a fisherman's house, before elders who can hold him to it. A vow with witnesses is hard to take back, and he seems to want it that way. The fisherman listens, and thanks him. Then he says there's one more thing he's worried about.
screen: `THE FISHERMAN'S PRAISE.` · `ONE FAULT: A RIVAL.` · `THE PROBLEM IS YOU.` · `I GIVE UP THE THRONE.` · then, large: `A VOW WITH WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Picture something that's yours, not something you'd lose in an emergency, just a seat, a title, a turn, a habit of being first, held in your closed hand. Breathe in and feel how naturally you hold it; breathe out and imagine opening the hand, just slightly. You don't have to give anything up, only notice what the open hand feels like.
Bhishma's vow. Its first part: before the elders, Devavrata gives up the throne so a fisherman's grandson can have it.
Your line: a vow with witnesses is hard to take back. Tomorrow, the fisherman's second worry. Day seven hundred twelve, done.

original.note: Sanskrit yuvarāja, the heir apparent: the place Shantanu gave Devavrata, and the place he gives up.

chat.says: Why did Devavrata make his promise in front of all those elders?
options: So it couldn't be taken back; a vow before witnesses binds you, and he wanted that.
Because the elders forced him to give up the throne against his own will.
Because his father ordered the elders to strike the bargain for him.
chat.meaning: Devavrata gave up the throne before chiefs who could hold him to it. A vow with witnesses is hard to take back.

yuvaraja.meaning: the heir apparent, the young king next in line
